clue.text: Like an incomplete sash — of lacklustre chintz?

definitions.meaning: a sash window missing its panes of glass
chintz is normally finished with a shiny glaze; dull chintz lacks that finish

explanation.surface: A dressmaker's riddle about an unfinished sash made of dull chintz fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sash' suggests a ribbon worn across the body, but here it is a sliding window frame.
explanation.definitionFit: A sash window without its panes has no glass fitted, and chintz without its usual polished coating is likewise without a glaze.

clue.text: Notably honest, not grand

definitions.meaning: a piano that stands vertically rather than a grand piano

explanation.surface: Someone is known for honesty but not for importance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grand' looks like an adjective for status; it is the grand piano, the opposite of the vertical sort.
explanation.definitionFit: A person of strict integrity is principled, and a vertical-strung piano is the alternative to the horizontal grand.

clue.text: Scenery for birdies including eagles

parts.note: birdies and eagles are golf scores below par, so their setting is a golf course

explanation.surface: A description of a habitat for small birds and birds of prey.
explanation.definitionFit: Birdies and eagles are scores achieved on a seaside golf course.

clue.text: This is the end whereby a feller gets his chips

definitions.text: This is the end whereby a feller gets his chips

parts.words: This is the end whereby a feller gets his chips
parts.note: a tree-feller's chips of wood come from the business end of his chopping tool, with a play on 'fellow' and 'getting one's chips' as dying

explanation.surface: A grim line about a man meeting his end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This is the end' and 'gets his chips' suggest death; 'feller' is a lumberjack, not a fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: The blade end of a woodcutter's chopping tool is what sends the wood chips flying.

clue.text: Real fractions of Flint's pieces

parts.note: Captain Flint's parrot squawks 'Pieces of eight!'; the old Spanish real was one part in eight of such a dollar

explanation.surface: A geologist's talk of genuine fragments of flint stone.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Flint is the parrot in Treasure Island crying 'Pieces of eight'; a real was a Spanish coin worth one part of eight.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish real was worth one part in eight of a peso, the 'piece of eight'.

clue.text: Jack Brown crossed, by design

parts.note: a jack, or jack tar, is a sailor, also called a tar
to brown in the sun is to tan; tan is a brown colour

explanation.surface: A man called Jack Brown was thwarted, perhaps deliberately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack Brown' looks like a person's name; it is two separate pieces, and 'crossed' describes a pattern of crossing stripes rather than someone thwarted.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish plaid is a woven pattern of stripes crossing at right angles.

clue.text: Young batrachian tail-shedder (after shedding it) on the Wharfe

indicators.note: the young frog loses its tail, so the final part of its name is dropped

parts.note: a tadpole is a young frog or toad, a batrachian
a caster is one who casts off or sheds something

explanation.surface: A young frog loses its tail by the River Wharfe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after shedding it' takes POLE (the tail end) off TADPOLE to leave TAD. The Wharfe is a Yorkshire river on which this brewing town stands.
explanation.definitionFit: This Yorkshire brewery town lies on the banks of that river.

clue.text: If securer maybe wouldn't have needed one

definitions.text: If securer maybe wouldn't have needed one

indicators.note: the word securer, maybe, could become another word if its letters were rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone safer would not have needed saving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' rearranges SECURER, and the whole clue also says someone safer would not need a saviour.
explanation.definitionFit: A person in danger needs a saviour; one safer would not.

clue.text: For Andy one dissolved to relieve pain

indicators.note: like a tablet dissolved in water, the letters of the words lose their shape and re-form

explanation.surface: A tablet is dissolved for Andy to ease his pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dissolved' rearranges ANDYONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A painkilling medicine is soothing; the word describes something that dulls discomfort.

clue.text: Would this describe a wedding ring dropped on a slope?

definitions.text: Would this describe a wedding ring dropped on a slope?

parts.words: Would this describe a wedding ring dropped on a slope?
parts.note: a ring falling on a slope would go trundling downhill, and a cheap ring of gilded base metal goes by a name describing exactly that

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what to call a wedding ring that has fallen on a hillside.
explanation.definitionFit: Base metal coated with a thin layer of the precious yellow metal goes by this name, and a dropped gold ring on a slope would literally be trundled.

clue.text: Showed we went out, but not barefoot

indicators.note: the letters of 'we' leave the word Showed, as if walking out of it

explanation.surface: Someone showed that we had gone out wearing footwear.
explanation.walkthrough: Take WE out of SHOWED and SHOD is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Wearing footwear, such as boots or shoes, is the opposite of going barefoot.

clue.text: Bardic cache of bullion shelved

definitions.meaning: Palgrave's famous anthology of English poems is a hoard of bards' work
a store of gold bars kept on shelves in a vault

explanation.surface: A poet's hidden stash of gold bars has been put away on a shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: Palgrave's anthology, a classic collection of English verse, is itself a book that sits on a shelf, which joins the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Palgrave's well-known poetry anthology carries this title, and literally the phrase means a stockpile of precious yellow metal.

clue.text: X does wrong in the island off Troy

parts.note: X is the Roman numeral for ten

indicators.note: done wrong, the letters of 'does' are put into a muddled order

explanation.surface: Someone called X behaves badly on an island near ancient Troy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' rearranges DOES into EDOS, which follows TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: This Aegean isle near the Turkish coast is where the Greeks hid their fleet during the Trojan War.

clue.text: Takes Hines's wicket — excels

parts.note: to take a batsman's wicket is to get him out, so 'takes ... wicket' means outs
Hines is the batsman's name, given as written

explanation.surface: A bowler dismisses a batsman named Hines and shines.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, to take someone's wicket is to get them out: 'Takes Hines's wicket' becomes 'outs Hines'.
explanation.definitionFit: To excel over others is to surpass them in brilliance.

clue.text: First course for cargo?

definitions.meaning: the opening dish of a meal
read as 'for car go': the device that makes a car go

explanation.surface: A question about which shipment goes first.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'cargo' into 'car go': the motor that gets an engine running.
explanation.definitionFit: A soup or appetiser opens a meal, and a motor's self-starting device gets a vehicle moving.

clue.text: Legume for Ann to bake perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the words could be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: A pod vegetable for Ann to cook in the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges ANNTOBAKE.
explanation.definitionFit: The seed of a South American tree used for flavouring is a pod-bearing plant's fruit.

clue.text: Daily so-called does

parts.note: a daily cleaner is known as a 'help', so the work such a person does is named after that title

explanation.surface: A remark on what a daily cleaning lady, as she is called, does.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'daily' is British slang for a cleaning woman who comes in each day, often called a home help.
explanation.definitionFit: A home help, as the cleaner is called, helps out, which is to aid or support.

clue.text: Audition of litter-leaver — hence no case for cash for QC

definitions.meaning: the organ of hearing of a pig that bears a litter of piglets

definitions.text: hence no case for cash for QC
definitions.meaning: proverbially you cannot make a silk purse out of it; a QC is a 'silk' and a purse is a case for cash

explanation.surface: A barrister hears there is no cash case to be made.
explanation.walkthrough: QC (Queen's Counsel) is a senior barrister, who 'takes silk'; you can't make a silk purse out of this.
explanation.definitionFit: A female pig's hearing organ, proverbially worthless material for a silk purse.

clue.text: Bury next turn of motorway, or betwixt and between

indicators.note: next places the second piece after the first

parts.note: to inter is to bury

indicators.note: the motorway's name is turned round to read backwards

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main motorway, written MI

explanation.surface: Instructions to bury something by the next motorway junction.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the London-to-Leeds motorway; read as MI and turned by 'turn of' it gives IM.
explanation.definitionFit: Something provisional comes in the intervening period between two states.

clue.text: Plan to turn the Gunners on to the target area

indicators.note: the abbreviation for the Gunners is turned round to face the other way

parts.note: RA, the Royal Artillery, are nicknamed the Gunners
a firing range is the area where targets are set up

explanation.surface: An order to swing the artillery round onto the firing range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to turn' makes RA into AR, placed before RANGE; 'on to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To plan something is to organise or set it out in order.

clue.text: In role of speaker, a trying man

parts.note: as means in the capacity or role of
a sayer is one who says something

explanation.surface: Someone playing a speaker's part who is tiresome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trying' suggests tiresome, but it means testing: one who tests metals.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who tests the purity of metals is in the business of testing or trying them.

clue.text: Bobs of "Queen's-shilling" days

parts.note: Bobs is a plural of Bob, a pet form of Robert, and 'Bobs' was the nickname of the Victorian field marshal Lord ..., from the era of the Queen's shilling recruitment

explanation.surface: A reminiscence about shillings from Queen Victoria's day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bobs' looks like shillings (a bob was slang for a shilling); taking the Queen's shilling meant joining the army.
explanation.definitionFit: Several men named Bob share one formal first name, and the Victorian field marshal nicknamed Bobs bore it as surname.

clue.text: Where that devious Heep's got us

indicators.note: devious means taking a crooked route, so the letters go round about to a new order

explanation.surface: A complaint about where a scheming man from a novel has led us.
explanation.walkthrough: Uriah Heep is the scheming clerk in Dickens's David Copperfield. 'devious' rearranges HEEPS and US.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancient Greek city in Asia Minor is a place, the 'where' of the clue.

clue.text: Hagmanay ?

parts.note: a made-up word blending 'hag' with Hogmanay, the Scottish New Year's Eve party: a festive night for crones

explanation.surface: A punning invented festival.
explanation.walkthrough: Hogmanay is the Scottish New Year's Eve celebration; swapping in 'hag' makes it a gathering of sorceresses.
explanation.definitionFit: A midnight gathering of sorceresses is the hags' version of a festive night.

clue.text: The honeyed one gets right bitter

parts.note: a bee is the insect that makes honey

explanation.surface: Someone sweet turns sour in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bitter' looks like an adjective for a mood but is a noun: the British pale ale.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitter is a type of British hoppy ale, a variety of the drink.

clue.text: White rose reinforcements from oversea?

parts.note: the white rose is the emblem of Yorkshire, so fresh recruits for that county would be new men of York; from overseas, they are citizens of the American city

explanation.surface: A Yorkshire side calls in extra players from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: The white rose is the emblem of Yorkshire, an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: Residents of the big American city, read literally as fresh men of the white-rose county.

clue.text: Little comfort for matey Bath chaps having drink taken

indicators.note: the companions are said to have something inside them
the drink is taken in, swallowed into the middle of the companions

parts.note: CBs are Companions of the Order of the Bath, so friendly 'companions' of the Bath
rum is a spirit drink

explanation.surface: Friendly chaps from Bath get little comfort from having a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: A CB is a Companion of the Order of the Bath, a British honour, hence 'matey' chaps; RUM goes inside CBS.
explanation.definitionFit: Small scraps of consolation are proverbially 'crumbs of comfort'.

clue.text: Tips for these makings of a legal document

definitions.text: these makings of a legal document
definitions.meaning: old deeds begin 'Know all men by these ...', the formal term for the document itself

explanation.surface: Advice on how to draft a legal document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips' looks like advice but means gifts; the phrase 'these presents' is old legal language for the deed in hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Gratuities are gifts, and in legal language the deed itself is called by this old term.
